critic_changes: All seven IMF passages and the EBRD passages were found verbatim in the opened PDFs, and every number in the prose matches desk/data/SVK.json (growth_problem and series).

EBRD citation dates changed from 2025-11-25 to 2025-11. The PDF does not print a day, its metadata gives a November 2025 date, and the publication page could not be re-opened to confirm the 25th, so the day is not guessed.

Arc and the 'Transition and EU gains fade' thread: removed the claim that the IMF links the 2001–2008 catch-up to the market transition and EU entry, and the claim that this era 'came after' joining the EU (EU entry fell in the middle of the era). The text now says the era covers the years around EU entry and gives the IMF's actual point: the gains from transition and EU entry are largely used up.
Shortened the first IMF quote in that thread to drop 'further income convergence depends on structural reforms', which is prescriptive.

'Ageing and slower productivity' thread: added the IMF passage 'Slovakia is particularly exposed to the challenges of an aging population', because no cited passage supported the claim that Slovakia is especially exposed.

'Car exports meet tariffs' thread: 'main export engine' changed to 'a key export engine', the EBRD's words. The IMF passage ties the automotive capacity expansion to rising imports, not to export growth, so the text now says exports grew strongly while imports rose as car plants added capacity.

'Energy dependence on Russia' thread: dropped the 2022–2023 consumer price figures. The data hold them, but no cited passage links inflation to energy dependence, so the sentence implied a cause the sources do not give.

since_last_year: replaced the EBRD quote ('The momentum of early 2025 has waned...') with the passage that actually names higher taxes and tariffs on the car industry, since the old quote did not support the claim. 'Budget cuts' became 'budget tightening', and 'household spending' became 'spending', to match 'fiscal consolidation' and 'consumption'.
Tension: dropped the sentence that the sources do not explain the 2009 drop. It describes a gap in the sources, not a disagreement between the sources and the data.

growth_story.headline: Slovakia caught up fast in the 2000s, but since 2009 income per person has grown 1.9 percent a year as gains from transition and EU entry faded.
growth_story.arc: Income per person fell 14.6 percent in 1991 and 6.8 percent in 1992, and despite a recovery in the middle of the decade the 1991–2000 era averaged just 0.7 percent a year. Growth then sped up to 6.2 percent a year over 2001–2008, the years around EU entry, peaking at 10.8 percent in 2007. Income per person fell 5.6 percent in 2009, and over 2009–2025 growth averaged 1.9 percent a year, with another dip of 2.7 percent in 2020. The IMF says catch-up with richer EU countries has slowed because the gains from the move to a market economy and from EU entry are largely used up, and that an ageing population and weaker productivity growth now weigh on growth. Growth averaged 2.0 percent a year over 2016–2025, down from 3.8 over 2006–2015, though income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Transition and EU gains fade
threads.text: Growth averaged 6.2 percent a year over 2001–2008, the years around EU entry. The IMF says the gains from the move to a market economy and from joining the EU are now largely used up, and that slowing growth has made it harder to close the income gap with richer EU countries.

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed in 2025: income per person rose 1.0 percent, after 2.0 percent in 2024. The IMF links the slowdown to budget tightening and weak consumer confidence, which held back spending. The EBRD adds higher taxes and US tariffs that hit the car industry.

citations.quote: the economy slowed in 2025, to 0.8 percent from 1.9 percent in 2024, as fiscal consolidation and subdued consumer confidence restrained consumption

citations.title: Transition Report 2025-26: Country assessments, Slovak Republic

growth_story.tension: The sources call 2025 a sharp slowdown, and the EBRD says the economy is stalling. The data still show income per person rising 1.0 percent that year to its highest level yet: slow growth, not a fall.
